title: Welfare-Optimal Classification with Accuracy Auctions
claim: A learning algorithm turns private values into welfare-maximizing allocations and sparse truthful payments, shown on one toy dataset.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right, same 2-D axes with evolving point encodings
description: Three side-by-side scatter plots share the same x1/x2 axes and the same toy 2-D dataset. The left panel, titled 'Input Features, Labels, and Bids', shows red and blue points, with point size encoding each participant's bid or value. The middle panel, 'Accuracy Allocation via Learning (SVM)', overlays a soft red/blue score-function heatmap and a dashed decision boundary. Points are green when correctly predicted and orange when not. A text annotation reads 'accuracy: 0.85; welfare: 91.8'. The right panel, 'Incentive-Compatible Payments', keeps the same background and boundary. It shows only a few magenta points, with size proportional to payment, and the annotation '#payers: 16; total pay: 7.0'. The eye goes first to the colorful points in the left panel, then follows the change across the panels from many points to a few payers.
caption: Accuracy auction induced by a classification algorithm. (Left) Each training point represents a participant in the auction: color represents label, and size represents value of accurate prediction. (Center) Welfare-maximizing allocation of pointwise accuracy via weighted loss minimization, showing learned score function (background color), decision boundary (dashed line), and prediction correctness (point color). (Right) User payments (size depicts magnitude) guarantee truthful elicitation, despite being highly sparse. \vspace{0em}
abstract: Prediction algorithms are increasingly used to inform decisions about humans, but maximizing accuracy-the standard learning objective-is not necessarily optimal for this purpose. Instead, we propose optimizing social welfare, defined as the average gain users receive from correct predictions. Welfare enables to express, and therefore account for, heterogeneity in how much users benefit from accuracy. But since these valuations are private and users can benefit from overreporting them, learning must simultaneously elicit truthful values and optimize welfare with respect to them. To this end, we propose a novel learning algorithm that incorporates a truthful auction. We show how to compute allocations and prices efficiently, and bound the number of paying users-which surprisingly is independent of the sample size. We conclude with experiments on real and synthetic data that demonstrate our algorithm and explore the connections between welfare and accuracy.
